extracted.intended_audience: philanthropists, foundation trustees, donors, and philanthropic administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and practical principles for creating, endowing, governing, and administering philanthropic endowments, pension funds, and charitable programs (trust structure, trusteeship, beneficiary selection, administration, and gift conditions). Drawn from practice-based examples and deed language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear institutional mission (deed language)
rubrics_metrics.description: The deed of gift should state a broad, liberal purpose for the institution (example wording: 'To encourage in the broadest and most liberal manner investigations, research and discovery, and the application of knowledge to the improvement of mankind; and, in particular, to conduct, endow and assist investigation in any department of science, literature or art, and to this end to coöperate with governments, universities, colleges, technical schools, learned societies, and individuals.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit mission language that allows cooperation with governments, universities, learned societies and individuals; frame objectives broadly enough to enable useful research and public-benefit activities without being unnecessarily restrictive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select distinguished, expert trustees
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose trustees from recognized leaders in relevant fields (e.g., presidents of educational institutions, leading scientists, statesmen) to guide and lend credibility to the fund.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie selected notable men (Presidents, cabinet-level figures, scholars) to serve as trustees; this both raised prestige and ensured wise oversight. For specific funds, set the trustee number appropriate to the purpose (e.g., twenty-five trustees for a university professors' pension fund).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant trustees authority to amend objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide trustees with the power to change objects of beneficence and modes of applying funds if original purposes become unsuitable or unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie initially proposed majority control but accepted a two-thirds requirement after discussion; including a supermajority requirement (e.g., two-thirds) can balance flexibility with protection against rash changes. Incorporate this provision into gift instruments for long-lived endowments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure endowments in durable instruments and allow growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Use secure financial instruments (e.g., bonds) for initial endowment gifts and allow additions to the capital contingent on recorded results or performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ten million dollars in five per cent bonds, later increased to a larger cash value as results justified. Design endowments to preserve capital and permit measured augmentation based on outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult political and subject-matter leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult relevant government leaders, subject experts, or statesmen when founding large public institutions to secure support and appropriate leadership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie consulted President Roosevelt and sought John Hay as chairman; such consultation can facilitate incorporation, legislative action (where needed), and higher public legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable formal cooperation with governments and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly provide in founding documents for cooperation with governments, universities, colleges, technical schools, learned societies and individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enables joint projects, use of expertise, and integration of institutional resources; state the cooperative intent in deed language to avoid later ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize recipients by need and likely impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct funds toward institutions or beneficiaries where marginal dollars produce greater social/educational return (e.g., smaller colleges and underpaid professors rather than already-large universities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie judged that smaller colleges were in greater need than large universities and adjusted grant focus accordingly. Consider empirical assessment of need and potential impact when choosing target recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create pension funds for deserving long-serving professionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish pension funds to provide for aged or disabled professionals (e.g., university professors, workmen, railroad employees) who cannot save adequately for old age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select trustees familiar with the profession; publish lists of beneficiaries where appropriate, but consider privacy. Carnegie's professors' pension fund used trustees drawn from university presidents and was viewed as remedial for low professional pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design rescue/hero funds as pensions, not bounties
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame awards for rescue or heroism as pensions or support for disabled heroes/their families, not as incentives intended to stimulate heroic acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie stressed the Hero Fund was intended to pension or provide for those disabled or killed in rescue efforts, and not to induce risky behavior by offering rewards. Clarify intent to avoid public misperception of perverse incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use local commissions/trustees for international administration
rubrics_metrics.description: When expanding funds internationally, appoint carefully chosen local commissions/commissions of experts and establish local headquarters to administer benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie extended the Hero Fund to many countries with local commissions that exchanged reports and coordinated; local administration improves cultural fit and operational effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exchange reports and coordinate across jurisdictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage commissions in different countries or regions to correspond, exchange reports, and learn from each other's experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal correspondence and sharing of case studies (as done between the American, English and German commissions) helps standardize best practices and improve decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appoint committed, capable administrators (sometimes from within)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select managers or presidents for funds who are devoted to the work; veterans or persons with long service and institutional memory can be effective leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Charlie Taylor, a Carnegie veteran, was chosen to lead pension operations and refused salary. Match role to person; consider incentives and whether a salary is appropriate or symbolic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require recipient cost-sharing to ensure prudent local commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Condition gifts (particularly capital items) on recipient contributions to ensure need, reasonable expenditure, and local buy-in (example: organ gifts required congregation to pay one half).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie required congregations to pay half the cost of a new organ to assure prudent spending and commitment; matching or cost-share requirements reduce waste and increase stakeholder responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematize application and graduation of gifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop standardized application procedures (printed schedules/questions) and scale gifts to recipient size or need (graduate gift size according to church or institution size).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A printed schedule requiring answers before action and graduated giving by size helped Carnegie's organ department operate efficiently. Standardization improves fairness and reduces ad hoc favoritism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use naming rights strategically and conditionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Donors may attach naming conditions to gifts (e.g., naming a building) as part of the gift agreement; this can help honor supporters and galvanize fundraising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie conditioned a Lehigh building on naming it 'Taylor Hall' to satisfy an advocate; donors should consider the reputational and motivational effects of naming and be prepared for recipient responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect beneficiary privacy for private pensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep private pension beneficiaries confidential when appropriate to protect dignity and avoid publicity for vulnerable recipients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie emphasized no publicity and confidentiality for his private pension list. Balance transparency (for accountability) with privacy and beneficiary dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate with other philanthropic funders to avoid duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate and coordinate with other major funders to ensure complementary activities and reduce undesirable overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie and Rockefeller operated in similar educational fields and later coordinated; early communication can reveal opportunities for cooperation or division of labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vet beneficiaries for merit and need
rubrics_metrics.description: Screen individuals and institutions to ensure beneficiaries are deserving and that assistance will be effectively used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie's private pension list comprised persons 'kind and good and in every way deserving.' Implement vetting criteria and processes to maintain program integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplement—not duplicate—employer or state support
rubrics_metrics.description: Design funds to complement existing employer, state, or private provisions (e.g., supplement what employers contribute to families after accidents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Hero Fund was intended to supplement employer contributions and provide support where those contributions were insufficient. Clarify the fund's relation to other social supports to avoid crowding out or duplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gift terms that create public misperception
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft public-facing terms (e.g., specific sums for individuals) to avoid creating impressions of impropriety or inequality; consider substituting vague but trusting language (e.g., 'suitable provision') if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie altered a specified lifelong stipend for Booker Washington to 'only suitable provision' at Washington's request to avoid the appearance of excessive personal enrichment; be sensitive to public perceptions when drafting individual provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use legal mechanisms appropriate to scale
rubrics_metrics.description: When necessary, use formal legal incorporation (or even act of legislation) to establish institutions and clarify powers, duties, and permanence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Carnegie Institution was incorporated by an act of Congress; for very large or national-level endowments, appropriate legal forms can secure longevity and authority.
